newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian party pushes for mercy killing law.
newsitem.headline: Australian party pushes for mercy killing law.

text.p: Australia's third-largest political party said on Saturday it would push for a popular vote across the country to allow assisted suicides after the Federal government quashed the world's first euthanasia law.
The leftist Australian Democrats, citing opinion polls showing overwhelming support for mercy killings, said the party wanted to put the issue in the hands of the people.
Their move was immediately welcomed by the doctor who helped in the world's only four legal voluntary euthanasia deaths before Canberra quashed a local law allowing assisted suicides.
"It's a way of toughening up some of the federal politicians who clearly didn't have the guts not to overturn (the law)," said Philip Nitschke, dubbed "Doctor Death" by critics.
"I am sure it will gain support from both conservative and Labor groupings," he told Reuters by phone from Darwin, capital of the Northern Territory.
The territory last year introduced a law which allowed assisted suicides, despite protests from pro-life and religious groups and vows by Prime Minister John Howard to overturn it.

The national parliament, using its constitutional powers over territories, last month narrowly voted down the Northern Territory law. But the government does not have the same power over Australia's six states, which enjoy more autonomy than the country's three territories.
Despite parliament's decision to quash the law, taken on a conscience vote rather than at party direction, polls show about 75 percent of Australians support euthanasia.

The Democrats, the third force in politics after the ruling coalition and the left-leaning Labor Party, will move for public votes in three states, including the most populous, New South Wales. "Everywhere I go, people are telling me a referendum is what they want," Democrats national leader Cheryl Kernot said.

Kernot's party will seek referendums in the Labor-governed New South Wales and in conservative-ruled South Australia and Western Australia. The Democrats will also push a national petition in favour of euthanasia.
Nitschke also hoped the push might help him win legal approval to help two more terminally ill patients to commit assisted suicide.
The two received approval under the short-lived Northern Territory euthanasia law, but were not ready to die before the national parliament overturned the law last month.
Nitschke said the popular backing for euthanasia meant success in just one state -- "where the federal government can't tamper with the law" -- would snowball into a nationwide win.
On Friday, legal authorities in Darwin refused to give Nitschke immunity if he helped his two patients die, he said.
"They are in an impossible situation," he said.
Four people committed assisted suicide, all helped by Nitschke, between the law coming into effect in July, 1996, and its quashing two weeks ago.
The territory law allowed dying patients who met strict guidelines and received the signed approval of three medical experts to commit suicide with the help of a doctor by lethal injection or pills.
